# Columns (TAB, exactly 5 on every data line; "-" = an empty field, since editors strip trailing TABs):
#   claim id | description (lines of v3.20; "fig_maxg1.tex l.N" = a line of the Figure 3 file) | REQUIRED rows | SUPPORT rows | KIND.
# KIND "-" = proved rows: status = worst REQUIRED row, hypotheses united (PROVED > PROVED GIVEN <facts/checks> > not
#   proved yet); every row carries, as explicit binders, every fact and check its proof uses.
#   FACT <Prop> = a fact the paper USES from an area Mathlib lacks: an explicit hypothesis in
#   Wills/Facts/Basic.lean, status "not formalized: no <area> in Lean's library".
#   CHECK <Prop>,<Prop> = a computer check: an explicit hypothesis in Wills/Checks/Computations.lean,
#   status "checked by computer, NOT proved in Lean" (log: ./reproduce.sh computation-N).
#   NOT-FORMALIZED faces = a claim about faces of polytopes: "not formalized: no faces of polytopes in Lean's library";
#   facets enter Lean only as the numbers of E3 (IsFacetData) and TRI.
# Quantifier rule: each printed quantifier and exception is compared with the row's type; a row true WITH an exception
#   does not cover a sentence WITHOUT it.
#   g_i = coefficient i of the interpolating polynomial of degree <= n through k = 0..n (EHR: it agrees with L at every
#   k >= 0); every sigma (or NVol) sentence is typed over E3's facet data, sigma = Σ relvol_j, NVol_j = 6 relvol_j, with
#   the fact FacetFormula as a binder (the real facets' data satisfy E3's equations, so the row implies the printed
# NOT COUNTED (no mathematical claim of this paper): history and attributions — abstract l.47 "In 1981 Wills
#   conjectured", "Wills proved this for n <= 3, and Henze showed in 2014 that it fails for every n >= 7; the dimensions
#   4, 5 and 6 remained open"; l.52 "Ehrhart [Ehr62] proved"; l.56 "may be negative [BR15]" (quoted, used by no proof);
#   l.58 "Wills looked for a discrete analog", "Wills called these numbers the expected values", "known as Wills'
#   conjecture", "We state it as in" [Hen14, Conjecture 1.1]; l.67 "Wills proved the case i = n-1 in every dimension" (the
#   attribution; the mathematics is claim I9c), "Wills also proved it for n = 3" (the mathematics is claim WIL3), the
#   dimension-4 bounds of [Wil81 Thm (iii)], "A discrete version of Minkowski's first theorem by" Betke, Henk and
#   Wills [BHW93, Theorem 2.1] "implies" L_P(k) <= L_{C_n}(k) ("which is the inequality of the conjecture
#   for the values of the two polynomials instead of their coefficients"), Henk-Schurmann-Wills [HSW05]
#   (a bound on g_{n-1} by successive minima, which implies Wills' bound), Henze's family P_n, P_7 and 1534/105 > 14,
#   Henze's root theorem, Bey-Henk-Wills [BHW07] "every such polytope is reflexive", Henze's Remark 2.2 quote;
#   Table 1 "before" column (the LEFT column) l.76-79; Figure 1 "Known before" row and caption l.140 first sentence;
#   l.151 "follows Averkov and Schymura", "who used it to compute the largest number of columns of a" Δ-modular integer
#   builds on that of Averkov, Borger and Soprunov"; l.248 "this is Wills' argument for
#   g_{n-1}"; l.163 "(Ehrhart, Macdonald)"; l.182 "cf. [Hen14, Prop 2.3]"; l.323 "(Minkowski [Min97]; see Venkov
#   [Ven54] and McMullen [McM80])"; l.367 "The search follows [AS24, Algorithm 1]"; Remark 7.3 l.415 "Alternatively, by
#   [BHW07] such a P would be reflexive" (a cited theorem that no proof uses; its last clause, the lattice distances 2

#   main ones; Table 1 and Figure 1 compare them; its third sentence is claim R2h); l.143 "is a computation";
#   l.151 "and they are enumerated by computer"; l.153 (what the expanded version [Goel26] contains); l.192; l.229

#   are W6b, W6c), the classes and "classes are recognized by a canonical form", "uses a different method, a sandwich
#   search"; l.367 and l.369 descriptions of the sandwich search (the two sets, the branching, "The search stops at

#   "All enumerations below are exhaustive and use exact integer and rational arithmetic", the repository "contains the

#   claims are F3a-F3g); Figure 3's caption "The dashed line is g_1 = 8", the grey and green dots (the drawing);

#   versions of the paper (last: v2.30 for the two Figure 3 rows, v2.80 for comp5_maximal). v2.30's claim W3c (l.220, int(2W)) left the text;
#   its row w_int2_all is SUPPORT of W3b.
#   Remarks about this Lean folder (no mathematical claim): the abstract's last sentence l.47 "The deduction of these

#   ("these results" = Theorems 1.2, 1.3, 7.1 and Corollary 1.4, the claims AB1-AB4; AUDIT.md lists each row's
#   hypotheses; the comparator words are printed only after `lake comparator` accepts the tagged tree); the footnote

column2: Abstract l.47 ("In dimension 4 the conjecture holds") + Table 1 l.76-77 + Theorem 1.2 l.93-95: every P in O^4 has g_1(P) <= 8 and g_2(P) <= 24; the abstract: Conjecture 1.1 holds for n = 4

Abstract l.47 + l.85 (Theorem 7.1 "determines the polytopes" P in O^4 with g_1(P) = 8) + Table 1 l.76 ("with equality exactly for C_4, a 24-cell T and a cross-polytope X, up to unimodular equivalence") + Theorem 7.1 l.383-385: up to unimodular equivalence, g_1(P) = 8 (P in O^4) only for the cube C_4, one explicit 24-cell T and one explicit cross-polytope X
Abstract l.47 + Table 1 l.78: a polytope W in O^5 with 50 vertices in [-1,1]^5 has g_1(W) = 101/10 > 10

Abstract l.47 + Table 1 l.78-79 ("counterexamples in every dimension n >= 5") + Corollary 1.4 l.105-107 + Figure 1 (l.113-140, "After this paper" row and the caption's second sentence: "This paper proves it for n = 4 (Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.4)" and disproves it for every n >= 5): Wills' conjecture holds in R^n (n >= 1) iff n <= 4
l.52-55 + l.158: Ehrhart's theorem — for a lattice Λ and a polytope P of dimension n with vertices in Λ, L_{P,Λ}(k) = #(kP ∩ Λ) is a polynomial in k >= 0 of degree n
l.56 + (E1) l.161: the leading coefficient g_n(P) is the volume (vol(P)/det Λ)
l.58: Minkowski's first theorem — a convex body K symmetric about 0 with no lattice point but 0 in its interior has volume <= 2^n, the volume of C_n
l.58: C_n belongs to O^n, L_{C_n}(k) = (2k+1)^n, so g_i(C_n) = 2^i binom(n,i)
l.67: for i = 0 there is equality (g_0(P) = g_0(C_n) for P in O^n)
l.67: for i = n the inequality is Minkowski's theorem (g_n(P) <= 2^n for P in O^n)
l.67: the case i = n-1 holds in every dimension; hence the conjecture holds for n <= 2

Theorem 1.2 l.93-95 (= AB1) + proof l.372-374 + Figure 2 l.277-288 (caption: G <= 29 by Lemma 4.3; for the others the integer functionals bounded by 1 decide which finite enumeration of Section 6 contains P, up to isomorphism; boxes: Case I -> Comp 1, Case II -> Comps 2, 3, Case III -> 39 classes of frame lattices -> Comps 4, 5)
l.151 (d): "In each case only finitely many sets of lattice points remain"
Theorem 1.3 l.98: W belongs to O^5; proof l.216: the 50 points lie in {-1,0,1}^5, form a symmetric set and span R^5, so Lemma 2.1 applies

Theorem 1.3 l.102 + proof l.222 + abstract l.47 "products with segments then give counterexamples in every dimension n >= 6" + l.143 "Products with segments carry the example to every higher dimension": for every n >= 6, W x C_{n-5} in O^n and g_1 = 101/10 + 2(n-5) = 2n + 1/10 > 2n = g_1(C_n), since g_1(C_m) = 2m
Table 2 caption l.196 + tab_witness.tex: W = conv of the 50 points ±p (p = the 25 listed points); all 50 points are vertices of W
Table 2 caption l.196: W has 92 facets, i.e. 92 hyperplanes H, each with W on one side, a point of W off H and 5 affinely independent vertices of W on H, no two with the same face W ∩ H
Table 2 caption l.196: these are all the facets of W (W has exactly 92)
Proof of Theorem 1.3 l.218: vol(W) = 386/15
l.220: the polynomial is determined by L_W(0) = 1 and L_W(1..5) = 117, 1815, 10765, 39927, 112639 (the row also states L_W(6) = 265705, which v2.80 no longer prints)

Corollary 1.4 proof l.109-111: n <= 3 Wills' theorem; n = 4: g_0 = 1 by (E1), g_3 <= 32, g_4 <= 16 by Minkowski, g_1, g_2 by Theorem 1.2; n >= 5: Theorem 1.3 gives a counterexample (route differences in the header)

Corollary 1.4 proof l.110 + l.67: Wills' theorem for n = 3 ([Wil81, Theorem (i), (ii)]): g_i(P) <= 2^i binom(3,i) for every P in O^3; the paper cites it, Lean proves it from the facts E1, E2, E3 (g_1 <= 6 from L(-1) = -1, 2 g_2 <= 3 g_3 and g_3 <= 8)
l.158: if phi is a linear isomorphism with phi(P) = P', phi(Λ) = Λ', then phi(kP) ∩ Λ' = phi(kP ∩ Λ) for every k, so L_{P',Λ'} = L_{P,Λ}
l.158: when Λ = Λ' = Z^n, the map phi lies in GL_n(Z)
(E2) l.162: reciprocity L_{P,Λ}(-k) = (-1)^n #(int(kP) ∩ Λ) for k >= 1

(E3) l.163 + l.167 + l.56 (g_{n-1} is half the lattice surface area): facets, primitive normals u_F, b_F integers (positive, the lattice distance, when 0 in int P), relvol(F) the (n-1)-dimensional volume of F "measured so that a fundamental domain of the lattice" Λ ∩ aff(F-F) "has volume 1"; g_{n-1} = sigma/2 and vol/det Λ = (1/n) Σ b_F relvol(F) when 0 in int P
(E4) l.164: L_{PxQ} = L_P L_Q, since k(PxQ) ∩ Z^{p+q} = (kP ∩ Z^p) x (kQ ∩ Z^q)
l.170: a polytope in O^n_Λ has dimension n, because 0 is an interior point
l.170 + l.151: G(P) is odd (the points other than 0 come in pairs ±x)

Lemma 2.2 l.182-188: P in O^p, Q in O^q ⇒ PxQ in O^{p+q} and g_1(PxQ) = g_1(P) + g_1(Q); proof: PxQ symmetric lattice polytope, int(PxQ) = int P x int Q

Remark 4.4 l.266: in dimension 4 the lower bound theorem proves (star) only when G <= 29 (3G - 13 > 6G - 102 iff G <= 29)
l.275: M(P) is finite (P contains a ball around 0) and symmetric; <u,x> in {-1,0,1} for u in M(P), x in P ∩ Z^4
